flow_helper:
function english_flow(labels,subtitles;title="")
    n=length(labels)
    p=plot(xlims=(0,n),ylims=(0,1),axis=false,grid=false,legend=false,title=title,
        size=(1100,260),margin=5Plots.mm)
    colors=["#d6efeb","#dce8fa","#ece0f6","#ffe9cf","#d6efeb"]
    for i in 1:n
        x=i-1
        plot!(p,Shape([x+.04,x+.88,x+.88,x+.04],[.33,.33,.76,.76]);
            fillcolor=colors[mod1(i,length(colors))],linecolor="#477086")
        annotate!(p,x+.46,.56,text(labels[i],10,"#142c43"))
        annotate!(p,x+.46,.17,text(subtitles[i],9,"#425d6f"))
        i<n && plot!(p,[x+.9,x+1.02],[.54,.54];arrow=true,color="#477086")
    end
    p
end

4.source:
## 2 · Give the learner enough ordinary sentences

[TinyStories](https://huggingface.co/datasets/roneneldan/TinyStories) is a public corpus of short
stories generated by GPT-3.5/GPT-4 using simple vocabulary. We use a bounded prefix of its
**GPT-4-only V2** files: 81,694 training stories, about 65.8 million normalized characters.
The [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.07759) studies small language models trained on this kind
of restricted language environment; its results do not guarantee what our one-hour experiment achieves.

Training text comes from the upstream training file. A separate prefix of the official validation
file is deduplicated against training and divided into **our own validation and test sets**.
Both have 2,581 stories. Exact normalized duplicates are removed; paraphrases can remain.
Bounded file prefixes are not a random sample of the entire released dataset.

We normalize punctuation and whitespace to ASCII for a transparent implementation. This changes the
original text. Source notices, hashes, filtering, and the CDLA-Sharing-1.0 data license are recorded
in `reference/datasets/english_basics/README.md` and `manifest.json`.

5.source:
split_names=["train","validation","test"]
story_counts=Int[]
character_counts=Int[]
for name in split_names
    lines=readlines(joinpath(DATA,name*".txt"))
    push!(story_counts,length(lines))
    push!(character_counts,sum(length,lines))
    @printf("%-10s %6d stories | %9d characters\n",name,length(lines),sum(length,lines))
end
training_lengths=length.(readlines(joinpath(DATA,"train.txt")))
p1=bar(split_names,story_counts;fillcolor=["#2c9e94","#5d85c6","#a88ac5"],legend=false,
    ylabel="Whole stories",title="Split documents before token windows")
p2=histogram(training_lengths;bins=40,color="#5d85c6",legend=false,
    xlabel="Normalized characters per story",ylabel="Stories",title="Short, simple texts for a small learner")
plot(p1,p2;layout=(1,2),size=(1100,380))

6.source:
## 3 · Tokens can be longer than characters

The first toy model predicted individual characters. Here we train **byte-pair encoding (BPE)**:
start with characters, repeatedly merge frequent adjacent pieces, and save the merge rules.
Common words or phrases may become a single token; uncommon words can still be assembled from pieces.

We first split text into words/numbers/punctuation with an optional leading space, then learn merges
within each piece. This keeps a word and its following space from being merged together, which is
helpful when a prompt ends at that word. We cap token length at 24 characters.
It is a teaching BPE, rather than an exact copy of GPT-2's tokenizer. It has 2,048 IDs, including
`<bos>` (beginning of a story), `<eos>` (end), and `<unk>` (unused for supported ASCII text).
Token IDs themselves have no numerical meaning. All vocabulary learning uses **training text only**.

The model predicts these pieces, so it does not have to reconstruct every common word one letter
at a time. It can still make up words or generate ungrammatical text; a tokenizer supplies no grammar rules.

7.source:
tok=load_bpe(DATA)
println("Julia/reference tokenizer agreement: ",check_bpe(tok,DATA)," cases passed")
text_example="The cat was happy."
example_ids=bpe_encode(tok,text_example)
println("Text:   ",repr(text_example))
println("Pieces: ",repr.(tok.tokens[example_ids]))
println("IDs:    ",example_ids)
@assert bpe_decode(tok,example_ids)==text_example
println("Character count: ",length(text_example)," | BPE token count: ",length(example_ids))

18.source:
## 8 · A real training run with a measured time budget

The trainer uses Adam, gradient norm clipping, a 150-step learning-rate warmup, then a cosine decrease
based on elapsed time. Parameters are stored in Float32; GPU matrix products may use TensorFloat32.
The first complete optimizer step is timed separately because compilation is expensive.

Validation uses fixed windows from unseen stories. It selects the checkpoint. The final test windows
are evaluated after selection and do not choose the best step. Model saving, the last validation,
and final samples get a two-minute reserve inside the 40-minute process budget.
The measured duration of the supplied run is printed below; other GPU workloads can change speed.

Set the switch to `true` to start from new random parameters. That replaces only this experiment's
`output/english_basics/` files. The earlier notebooks and their checkpoints remain separate.

20.source:
## 9 · Inspect learning, then inspect language

Training loss measures fit to seen text; validation measures prediction on held-out stories.
A growing gap is evidence of overfitting. Perplexity is `exp(loss)` and is measured **per BPE token**.
It cannot be directly compared with the earlier character model's perplexity.

These losses use fixed sampled windows, rather than an exhaustive whole-corpus likelihood.
Lower loss helps, but the next section checks actual sentences for grammar and continuity.

21.source:
history=trained.history
steps=[h.step for h in history]
tr=[h.train_loss for h in history]
va=[h.validation_loss for h in history]
p1=plot(steps./1000,tr;label="Training windows",color="#2c9e94",
    xlabel="Thousands of optimizer updates",ylabel="Cross-entropy / BPE token",title="Real learning curves")
plot!(p1,steps./1000,va;label="Validation windows",color="#5d85c6")
vline!(p1,[trained.metadata["best_step"]/1000];label="Selected checkpoint",color="#aa7caf",linestyle=:dot)
lr_history=[h for h in history if h.learning_rate>0]
p2=plot([h.seconds/60 for h in lr_history],Float64[h.learning_rate for h in lr_history].*1000;
    color="#bc874f",legend=false,xlabel="Elapsed minutes",ylabel="Learning rate × 1,000",title="Learning rate decreases with the budget")
@printf("Best validation CE %.4f | final test CE %.4f | test BPE perplexity %.2f\n",
    trained.metadata["best_validation_loss"],trained.metadata["test_loss"],exp(trained.metadata["test_loss"]))
@printf("Training tokens processed: %.2f million\n",trained.metadata["tokens_processed"]/1e6)
plot(p1,p2;layout=(1,2),size=(1150,400),left_margin=12Plots.mm,bottom_margin=13Plots.mm)

22.source:
### The embeddings changed without being assigned semantic labels

The two panels use the same color scale and show the first eight coordinates of the same token pieces.
Coordinates moved because prediction errors flowed back through the network. This demonstrates
learning; it does not identify human-readable meanings for those axes.

23.source:
shown_ids=unique(vcat(bpe_encode(tok,"The little cat was happy."),bpe_encode(tok,"One day, a dog said hello.")))[1:10]
E0=initial.model.tokens.weight[1:8,shown_ids]
E1=model.tokens.weight[1:8,shown_ids]
limit=max(maximum(abs,E0),maximum(abs,E1))
piece_labels=replace.(tok.tokens[shown_ids]," "=>"·")
p0=heatmap(piece_labels,1:8,E0;clims=(-limit,limit),color=:RdBu,colorbar=false,
    xlabel="Token piece (· is a space)",ylabel="Embedding coordinate",title="Random initialization",xrotation=30)
p1=heatmap(piece_labels,1:8,E1;clims=(-limit,limit),color=:RdBu,
    xlabel="Token piece (· is a space)",ylabel="Embedding coordinate",title="Trained checkpoint",xrotation=30)
@printf("Embedding-table movement norm: %.4f\n",norm(model.tokens.weight-initial.model.tokens.weight))
plot(p0,p1;layout=(1,2),size=(1150,430),bottom_margin=20Plots.mm)

24.source:
## 10 · Read the actual continuations

The prompts below are supplied text. Everything after `CONTINUATION:` is produced by the model.
We use a fixed prompt list, fixed seeds, temperature 0.65, and top-k 40. There is no rewriting or
searching over seeds for better answers. The first sample shows the random model before training.
That random sample may already contain English words because BPE pieces were learned from real text;
the untrained network has not yet learned how to arrange those pieces into sensible sentences.

Temperature changes randomness, not knowledge. Lower values concentrate the probabilities and can
increase repetition; higher values can produce more variety and more mistakes. An end marker stops
generation; otherwise the sample ends at the token limit, possibly in the middle of a sentence.

25.source:
prompt_list=["Once upon a time, there was a little","The cat looked at the dog and said,",
    "One day, a little girl found a","\"Hello,\" said Tom. \"How are you?\""]
untrained_sample=sample_text(initial.model,tok;prompt=prompt_list[1],seed=8,max_new=35)
println("BEFORE TRAINING\nPROMPT: ",untrained_sample.prompt,"\nCONTINUATION: ",untrained_sample.continuation,"\n")
generated=[sample_text(model,tok;prompt,seed=7+i,max_new=110) for (i,prompt) in enumerate(prompt_list)]
for (i,s) in enumerate(generated)
    println("AFTER TRAINING — sample ",i,"\nPROMPT: ",s.prompt,"\nCONTINUATION: ",s.continuation,
        "\nEnded at story end: ",s.ended_at_eos," | New tokens: ",s.new_tokens,"\n")
end

26.source:
### Fluent text can still be copied, repetitive, or inconsistent

Evaluate spelling, grammar, and whether each sentence follows the previous one. Separately check
whether the model repeats familiar training text. The following exact-substring diagnostic checks
only whether a generated passage of at least 80 characters appears verbatim in training.
Failure to find one does not prove originality: altered wording or memorized fragments may remain.

27.source:
training_text=read(joinpath(DATA,"train.txt"),String)
for (i,s) in enumerate(generated)
    passage=strip(s.continuation)
    if length(passage)<80
        println("Sample ",i," is too short for the long-passage copying check.")
    else
        println("Sample ",i," long exact training substring: ",occursin(passage,training_text))
    end
end

28.source:
## 11 · Look inside one learned attention head

This figure is measured from the **trained first layer**, not drawn as an illustrative weight pattern.
Rows are keys being read; columns are queries making predictions. Future entries remain zero.
One head's weights describe one information-routing step; they do not by themselves explain the
whole model's final choice or establish that it understands a word.

29.source:
attention_ids=vcat(tok.bos,bpe_encode(tok,"The small cat looked at the dog."))
T_attn=length(attention_ids)
H=model.tokens(reshape(attention_ids,:,1)) .+ reshape(model.positions(collect(1:T_attn)),256,T_attn,1)
block=model.blocks[1]
Z=block.norm1(H)
Q=JokesGPT.split_heads(block.attention.query(Z),8)
K=JokesGPT.split_heads(block.attention.key(Z),8)
scores=Flux.NNlib.batched_mul(permutedims(K,(2,1,3)),Q)./sqrt(32f0)
weights=Flux.softmax(scores.+reshape(causal_mask(T_attn),T_attn,T_attn,1);dims=1)
labels=replace.(tok.tokens[attention_ids]," "=>"·")
heatmap(labels,labels,weights[:,:,1];clims=(0,1),color=:blues,
    xlabel="Query: position making the prediction",ylabel="Key: position being read",
    title="Trained first layer, attention head 1",xrotation=35,
    size=(950,550),bottom_margin=23Plots.mm,left_margin=20Plots.mm,colorbar_title="Weight")

30.source:
## 12 · Check that prediction does not read the answer

Change future input IDs and require earlier logits to stay fixed. Also compare a prefix predicted on
its own with its predictions inside the full sequence. These numerical checks test the causal mask,
not fluency. Loading the saved reference also checks the checkpoint's CPU predictions.

31.source:
reference=deserialize(joinpath(OUT,"verification_probe.jls"))
probe=reference.probe
T_probe=size(probe,1)
L=predict(model,probe,causal_mask(T_probe),collect(1:T_probe))
changed=copy(probe)
changed[4:end,1].=tok.eos
Lc=predict(model,changed,causal_mask(T_probe),collect(1:T_probe))
Lp=predict(model,probe[1:3,:],causal_mask(3),collect(1:3))
future_effect=maximum(abs.(L[:,1:3,:]-Lc[:,1:3,:]))
prefix_error=maximum(abs.(L[:,1:3,:]-Lp))
reload_error=maximum(abs.(L-reference.logits))
@printf("Future-input effect: %.3g | prefix difference: %.3g | CPU checkpoint reference: %.3g\n",
    future_effect,prefix_error,reload_error)
@assert future_effect<1f-5
@assert prefix_error<1f-4
@assert reload_error<1f-5
@assert norm(model.tokens.weight-initial.model.tokens.weight)>0
println("Causal prediction and learned-embedding checks passed.")

32.source:
## 13 · A small grammar probe

Does the prefix `The cats` make the model prefer ` are` over ` is`? Each alternative below is a
single BPE token. We restrict the comparison to those two choices and report

$$P(\text{correct}\mid\text{correct or incorrect})=
\frac{\exp(z_{correct})}{\exp(z_{correct})+\exp(z_{incorrect})}.$$

This tests a few handpicked subject–verb agreement patterns. It is not a standardized grammar
benchmark or proof of general fluency. Some prefixes are less typical story openings than others.
The random model provides a before-training comparison using exactly the same tokenizer.

33.source:
grammar_cases=[("She"," is"," are"),("He"," has"," have"),("They"," are"," is"),
    ("We"," are"," is"),("I"," am"," are"),("The cat"," is"," are"),
    ("The cats"," are"," is"),("The dog"," has"," have"),("The dogs"," have"," has"),
    ("The little girl"," is"," are"),("The little girls"," are"," is"),("The two boys"," are"," is")]
function agreement_probability(m,prefix,correct,wrong)
    @assert haskey(tok.bytext,correct) && haskey(tok.bytext,wrong)
    ids=vcat(tok.bos,bpe_encode(tok,prefix))
    T=length(ids)
    z=vec(predict(m,reshape(ids,:,1),causal_mask(T),collect(1:T))[:,end,1])
    Flux.softmax(z[[tok.bytext[correct],tok.bytext[wrong]]])[1]
end
before=[agreement_probability(initial.model,c...) for c in grammar_cases]
after=[agreement_probability(model,c...) for c in grammar_cases]
labels=[prefix*":"*correct for (prefix,correct,wrong) in grammar_cases]
for (c,p) in zip(grammar_cases,after)
    @printf("%-18s prefers %-5s over %-5s: %5.1f%% (two-choice probability)\n",c[1],c[2],c[3],100p)
end
println("Correct alternative preferred: ",count(>(.5),after)," / ",length(after)," handpicked cases")
x=collect(eachindex(grammar_cases))
p=bar(x.-.18,before;bar_width=.32,label="Random weights",color="#a9bdca")
bar!(p,x.+.18,after;bar_width=.32,label="Trained weights",color="#2c9e94",
    xticks=(x,labels),xrotation=40,ylims=(0,1.12),ylabel="Two-choice probability of correct verb",
    title="A narrow agreement check, not a general English exam",size=(1200,480),bottom_margin=28Plots.mm)
hline!(p,[.5];label="Equal preference",linestyle=:dash,color="#a77c50")
